content: Atropine at a dose of 0.25 mg is included in this medication as part of a Schedule IV combination approved by the US FDA. The purpose of adding atropine is to reduce the potential for misuse, as diphenoxin, a component of the medication, is chemically related to the opiate family and could theoretically be abused. Although misuse or abuse is rare and unlikely, physical withdrawal symptoms may still occur if the medication is taken for extended periods. Both atropine and diphenoxin contribute to the therapeutic effects of the medication by slowing intestinal motility. It is important to note that this combination medication should not be confused with Lomotil, as the active ingredients differ, except for the inclusion of atropine. Motofen is officially indicated by the FDA for the treatment of diarrhea. However, it has also been successfully used by physicians to manage symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and hyperhidrosis (a condition characterized by chronic, severe sweating). The side effects of this medication include, but are not limited to, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, burning eyes, blurred vision, dry eyes, dizziness, dry mouth, epigastric distress, and constipation (a paradoxical side effect). Additional side effects, particularly those caused by atropine, may include flushing, dryness in various areas, urinary retention, insomnia, headache, anxiety, hyperthermia, and tachycardia. These atropine-related side effects make it undesirable for most patients to take higher doses of the medication. The initial dosing recommendation is two tablets to be taken at the start, followed by one tablet after each loose stool. The maximum recommended therapeutic dosage of Motofen is eight tablets (equivalent to 8 mg of diphenoxin). There are no specific dosing instructions for its use in IBS or hyperhidrosis, although it has been successfully used to treat symptoms of both conditions, which can sometimes occur together. A Motofen half-strength tablet, containing 5 mg of diphenoxin but the same amount of atropine, was previously available but has since been discontinued. The 0.25 mg strength tablets are still available by prescription. Currently, Motofen is manufactured exclusively by Valeant Pharmaceuticals, which acquired the drug from Amarin Pharmaceuticals in 2004. The tablets are pentagonal in shape, debossed with a V on one side, and vertically scored on the other side. The number 0500 is debossed across the score line, with 05 and 00 appearing on the left and right sides, respectively. Motofen is more expensive than both Imodium and Lomotil, lacks a generic equivalent, and is only available by prescription in the United States. Most US insurance companies do not include Motofen in their formulary, leading to high copays for consumers if it is covered at all. The United States is currently the only country where Motofen is prescribed, government-approved, and sold. This is likely due to its high cost and the availability of lower-priced alternatives for managing diarrhea symptoms. However, loperamide and Lomotil appear to be less effective, if effective at all, in treating IBS and hyperhidrosis. Interestingly, Motofen was only included in the Physicians' Desk Reference (PDR) for the years 2005 and 2006, and even then, only as a brief snippet entry. The PDR listing provided information on the ingredients, appearance at the time of publication, NDC number, and supply quantities, but did not include details on indications or usage. Despite this, Motofen remains available and is not particularly difficult to find in pharmacies located in reasonably sized metropolitan areas. However, pharmacists may be unfamiliar with the medication and surprised to find it on their shelves.
